item.research_question: How can room-temperature deformation twinning be induced in a high-entropy alloy to improve cryogenic tensile properties, and can non-recrystallized grains be utilized to achieve ultra-high yield strength while maintaining ductility?
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization at 1,100 °C for 6 h; cold rolling at room temperature with a 75% reduction ratio to produce 1.5-mm-thick sheets; annealing at 750 °C for 10 min to obtain partially recrystallized microstructure (H750) or at 900 °C for 10 min for fully recrystallized microstructure (H900); water quenching.
item.test_conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature and cryogenic temperature (−196 °C) using a crosshead speed of 6.4 × 10−3 mm s−1.
key_findings: The H750 alloy achieved a yield strength of 970 MPa and a tensile strength of 1,314 MPa at cryogenic temperatures.
The H750 alloy maintained a persistent elongation of 46.3% at cryogenic temperatures.
Non-recrystallized grains in the H750 alloy had an average size of ~32 μm, while recrystallized grains averaged ~1.5 μm.
Deformation twins with thicknesses of 10–30 nm were observed in recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.
Primary twin bundles of ~500 nm thickness and secondary twins of 30–70 nm thickness formed in non-recrystallized grains at cryogenic temperatures.
The yield strength of the H750 alloy was ~270 MPa higher than that of the fully recrystallized H900 alloy at cryogenic temperatures.
Room-temperature cold rolling induced deformation twins in coarse grains without prior hot rolling, which were retained after partial recrystallization.
item.mechanism: The critical stress for twinning decreases with increasing grain size, allowing twins to form readily in coarse non-recrystallized grains during cold rolling at room temperature. These retained twins act as strong barriers against mobile dislocations, enhancing yield strength. At cryogenic temperatures, additional deformation twins form in both recrystallized and non-recrystallized regions, leading to a high strain-hardening effect and ultra-high strength.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that non-recrystallized regions are generally avoided in conventional alloys due to deleterious effects on ductility.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the combination of room-temperature deformation twinning and non-recrystallization offers a strengthening mechanism for ultra-high-strength HEAs and suggest the alloy is promising for applications in ultra-high-strength HEAs at cryogenic temperatures.
quotes: Our results demonstrate that non-recrystallized grains, which are generally avoided in conventional alloys because of their deleterious effect on ductility, can be useful in achieving high-strength high-entropy alloys.
The persistent elongation up to 46% as well as the tensile strength of 1.3 GPa are attributed to additional twinning in both recrystallized and non-recrystallization regions.
As the grain size increases, σT becomes smaller than σS, which provides a good explanation for the profuse twinning at large grains.
